analysis.one_liner: Requires new vehicles to detect people and objects in front of them to prevent frontover deaths.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A frontover is when a slow-moving car strikes a person, usually a child, in the blind zone directly in front of the hood. This bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write a safety standard requiring vehicles to carry technology — cameras, sensors, or anything that works — so drivers can detect people and objects in front of the vehicle before moving. It also would have added frontover and backover incidents to the federal database that tracks non-traffic deaths and injuries. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with small children, especially those near large vehicles like pickups and SUVs, where the front blind zone hides a child standing close to the bumper. Pedestrians, wheelchair users, cyclists, and pet owners would also gain from a required forward perception zone. Vehicle buyers would get the protection as standard equipment on new cars.

how_it_helps.text: Directs DOT to write a federal motor vehicle safety standard requiring a perception zone in front of the vehicle so the driver can detect and respond to objects before a frontover or low-speed forward-moving incident [S2][S3].

Lets automakers meet the standard with any technology that works — sensors, cameras, or other means — and allows the Secretary to phase in compliance by vehicle type, prioritizing the types most often involved in frontover deaths [S3].

Adds frontover and backover incidents to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's Non-Traffic Surveillance System, so the government would finally count and publish data on these deaths [S2][S3].

Puts the rule on a clock: rulemaking within one year, a final standard within two, and full manufacturer compliance within two years after that, with 90-day reports to Congress if the Department falls behind [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers would bear the cost of adding cameras, sensors, or other detection equipment to every new vehicle, some of which would likely show up in vehicle prices. The Department of Transportation would take on the cost of writing and enforcing a new safety standard and expanding its crash data collection.

drawbacks.text: A mandate covering most vehicles on the road would impose engineering and equipment costs on manufacturers, some portion of which is typically passed through to new-vehicle prices [S3].

Frontover incidents are counted separately only if the data system is updated first, meaning the scale of the problem — and the benefits of the mandate — would rely on reporting that the bill itself has to create [S3].

The bill sets hard deadlines — one year to start, two years to finish the rule — that are fast by federal safety-standard standards, and allows only 90-day reporting rather than a change if the Department cannot meet them [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is straightforward: frontovers kill and injure small children at low speeds in spaces drivers cannot see, and the same technology already mandated for backup cameras can address the front blind zone. The main cost is per-vehicle equipment expense passed to buyers, and the bill's tech-neutral, phase-in design gives manufacturers room to comply cheaply. The chief weakness is not the policy but the process: the bill never got a hearing or a single cosponsor, so Congress never weighed these trade-offs at all.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the 117th Congress ended, never reaching a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Blumenthal introduced the STOP Frontovers Act on November 14, 2022, near the end of the second session of the 117th Congress [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day of introduction [S5].
The committee took no further action, and no vote ever occurred in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off because the bill died: they face no new mandate to equip vehicles with front-facing detection technology. Families at risk of frontover incidents gained nothing, and the government still does not track these incidents the way the bill required.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor; it was referred to the Commerce Committee the same day.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred; took no further action
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on November 14, 2022, and never held a hearing or advanced it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so it never developed support in either caucus.

industries.note: The bill would have required every new car, pickup, and SUV to carry forward detection technology, an engineering and equipment cost the industry avoids because the bill died. Its cost is the safety gain the public forgoes.
A tech-neutral mandate for forward perception zones would have created a guaranteed market for the same camera and sensor hardware now standard for backup views.
